hotel-promotional-package-guest-awarenes.titleEn: Why Do Guests Still Not Know About a Hotel's Promotional Packages After They Launch?
hotel-promotional-package-guest-awarenes.description: 套餐上线不等于完成推广。酒店需要把广告触达、员工介绍和预订前后信息接成一条完整的客人决策与使用链。

hotel-promotional-package-guest-awarenes.author: MarvelBros C&T（MarvelBros C&T）
content: 酒店推广套餐做出来了，为什么客人还是不知道？
会议室里的PPT已经讲完，核算表上的数字也算清了，内部通知邮件发到了各部门。从流程上看，一个暑期套餐已经"上线"了。但如果此时打开酒店预订页面、搜索入口或者致电前台，客人大概率仍然看不到它，或者看到了也说不清它到底包含什么、适合谁、怎么用。
套餐上线不等于完成推广。酒店需要让广告说清这个产品适合谁，让员工讲清为什么值得选，让客人在预订前后就知道包含什么、如何使用、有什么边界。这三件事缺任何一件，套餐就只是内部文件里的一个条目，而不是客人能感知到的一个选择。
我们来看一个典型经营场景。某酒店完成了暑期亲子套餐的设计：包含住宿、早餐、儿童乐园体验和一份延迟退房权益。PPT汇报通过，价格核算完成，内部通知已发。但一周过去，预订量远低于预期。问题不在产品本身，而在于这个套餐从设计完成到客人真正看见之间，存在多个没有被接上的断点。
第一个断点：广告只罗列了权益和折扣，没有说清客群和场景
打开这个套餐的推广页面，标题写的是"暑期特惠套餐"，正文列出了四项权益和原价对比。信息没有错，但也没有回答客人最关心的问题：这个套餐适合谁？什么情况下选它比单订房间更合适？延迟退房到底能延到几点？儿童乐园是否需要预约？
当广告只停留在"有什么"和"省多少"，客人需要自己去猜适不适合。而大多数客人不会猜，他们会直接划走。
第二个断点：员工知道价格和权益，但不知道怎么帮客人匹配
前台和预订部同事收到了内部通知，知道套餐价格和包含内容。但当客人打电话来问"带孩子住两晚有什么推荐"时，员工往往只会报价格，或者机械地念一遍权益清单。他们缺少一张简单的介绍卡：什么类型的客人适合推荐这个套餐、推荐时用哪句话开头、客人如果犹豫最常见的顾虑是什么以及怎么回应。
员工不是不愿意推荐，而是没有被给予一个足够简单的推荐路径。
第三个断点：客人在预订后、到店前、到店时，都没有收到清晰的使用说明
客人下单之后收到的确认信息里，套餐内容只有一行摘要。到店前没有提醒告知儿童乐园的预约方式。前台办理入住时也没有主动说明延迟退房的使用条件和申请方式。客人可能直到离店那天才想起来自己买过一个权益，但已经来不及用了。
信息传达的缺失，让已经购买的客人也无法完整体验套餐内容，更谈不上复购和推荐。
把这三条线接起来
要解决这些问题，不需要推翻已有的套餐设计，而是把四个环节连成一条完整的线。
第一步，明确客群与场景。这个套餐主要面向哪类客人？是本地家庭周末短住，还是外地游客的亲子行程？不同客群关注的重点不同，广告语言和员工推荐话术也应该不同。
第二步，重写广告核心信息。标题直接点明客群和场景，正文用客人能感知的语言描述体验，而不是用内部术语罗列权益。价格对比可以保留，但不要让它成为唯一的说服逻辑。
第三步，制作员工介绍卡。一张卡片只写三件事：适合什么样的客人、推荐时第一句话说什么、客人最常见的三个疑问和对应回答。不需要长篇培训手册，关键是让员工快速确认如何开口。
第四步，补齐预订后的客人信息链。确认订单时发送套餐使用须知，到店前一天发送预约提醒和注意事项，办理入住时前台用一句话确认客人已了解核心权益。这条信息链的成本很低，但直接影响客人能不能真正用到自己买到的东西。
读者现在就可以做的一件事
选一个已经上线但销售不及预期的套餐，用一位真实目标客人的身份走一遍完整路径：搜索时能不能看到它？看到时能不能快速判断适不适合自己？打电话给前台时员工能不能用一句话讲清楚？下单后收到的信息够不够用？走完这四步，多数推广链路中的薄弱环节会更容易被识别出来。
怎么验证推广是不是真的在起作用
不需要复杂的系统，分层记录就够了。广告触达了多少人？页面咨询了多少次？员工主动推荐了多少次？客人能不能说清自己买了什么？实际兑换率是多少？履约过程中出现了哪些问题？离店后评价反馈提到了什么？这些数据不需要每天分析，但需要有人每周看一次，才能知道哪一段在漏。
常见问题

套餐上线多久没效果就该调整？
  如果上线一周后预订量明显低于预期，建议先检查广告信息和员工推荐路径，而不是急着改价格或换产品。

员工培训需要多长时间？
  如果介绍卡做得足够简单，一次简短的班前会即可用于完成第一轮对齐。关键是卡片本身要足够具体，而不是泛泛地说"主动推荐"。

广告信息应该多久更新一次？
  建议定期查看广告页面的咨询转化情况。如果咨询量正常但预订量不高，问题可能在页面内容；如果咨询量本身就低，问题可能在投放渠道或标题吸引力。

预订后的信息传达会不会打扰客人？
  关键信息不是打扰，是服务。预约提醒、使用须知和权益说明属于客人已经购买的内容，在合适的时间点发送只会提升体验。真正会打扰客人的是频率过高或与套餐无关的营销信息。

如果套餐本身设计就有问题怎么办？
  推广能解决的是"让对的人看见并对的产品被理解"。如果产品本身与客群需求不匹配，推广做得再好也只能短期拉动。建议先做一次小范围的客群验证，再决定是否大规模推广。

contentEn: Why Do Guests Still Not Know About a Hotel's Promotional Packages After They Launch?

The PPT in the meeting room is finished. The cost spreadsheet is signed off. The package has a name, a price, and a start date. And yet the guest sitting on your booking page, or the one on the phone asking what's available this weekend, has no idea the package exists. Somewhere between the internal launch and the guest's screen, the whole thing quietly disappeared.

Here is the short answer. Launching a package is not the same as completing its promotion. A package is only "promoted" when three things are true at the same time: the advertising makes clear who the package is for, the front-line staff can explain why a specific guest should choose it, and the guest knows before and after booking what is included, how to use it, and where the boundaries are. If any one of these is missing, the package can be fully built inside the hotel and still be invisible to the people who would actually buy it.
A typical operating scenario

Consider a common summer situation, the kind you'll find in many hotels rather than any single client. A property builds a summer family package. The internal work is thorough: the deck is polished, the costing is careful, the internal notice goes out to every department. Everyone inside the hotel knows the package launched. But the package never enters the guest's information flow. It doesn't appear clearly on the booking channels guests actually use, the reception team can recite the price but not the fit, and the confirmation and pre-arrival messages say nothing about it. The package exists. The guest never meets it.
Three breakpoints where packages disappear

The first breakpoint is the advertising itself. Most package ads list benefits and discounts, and stop there. "Buy the summer package and get breakfast for two, a late checkout, and a welcome fruit plate." What's missing is the segment and the scenario. Who is this for? A family with young children? A couple on a short break? Guests arriving late by train? Without a clear "this is for you" signal, a guest reading the ad has no reason to feel it was written for them, so they scroll past.

The second breakpoint is the staff introduction. Front-line teams often know the price and the list of benefits, but not how to match the package to the guest in front of them. When a guest calls and describes their trip, the useful move is to connect their situation to the right package. Instead, staff frequently default to quoting the standard room rate, because that's the safe answer they're sure about. The package is technically available, but it's never offered at the moment it would have mattered.

The third breakpoint is the guest information delivery after booking. Even when a guest does buy the package, the booking confirmation, the pre-arrival reminder, and the on-site guidance often fail to clarify how to actually use it. Which restaurant honors the breakfast? Until what time is the late checkout? Does the welcome gift need to be requested at the desk? When usage details are unclear, guests either don't redeem what they paid for or feel confused at the property, and both outcomes quietly erode the package's value.
Connecting the three lines
These three breakpoints are really one broken chain, and it can be reconnected deliberately.

Start with a guest segment and scenario table. For each package, write down the one or two guest types it truly serves and the situations they're in. This single document becomes the source for everything downstream.
From that table, define the ad's core message. Not a longer list of perks, but a clear opening line that names the guest and the scenario, so the right reader recognizes themselves immediately.

Give the front desk and reservations team a staff introduction card. One short reference per package: who it fits, the one sentence that explains why, and the natural moment to bring it up in a conversation.

Then build the post-booking guest information chain. The confirmation, the pre-arrival message, and the on-site guidance should each carry the same practical usage details, so the guest always knows what's included, how to use it, and what the limits are.
What the reader can do today

Pick one package you've already launched. Don't rebuild it. Instead, trace it along a real target guest's path: search and browsing, the ad they'd see, the phone or desk conversation, the booking confirmation, the pre-arrival message, and arrival at the property. At each step, ask a simple question. Would this guest know the package exists, understand it's for them, and know how to use it? The first place the answer becomes "no" is your first breakpoint.
Verifying that promotion is actually working

Because "we launched it" tells you nothing about whether guests found it, promotion effectiveness is worth checking in layers. Look at ad reach, at whether the booking pages generate inquiries, at whether staff are actually recommending the package, at whether guests understand what they bought, at actual redemption of the included items, at any fulfillment issues on site, and finally at what guests say in reviews. A package can pass the first layer and fail the fourth, and only layered tracking shows you where.
How MarvelBros C&T works on this

MarvelBros C&T (MarvelBros C&T) approaches this as a chain rather than a single fix. The work typically covers product sorting to clarify who each package serves, a diagnosis of ad and channel content to see what guests actually encounter, a review of the staff introduction process so the right package is offered at the right moment, and a check of the guest information chain and its effect after booking. The aim is straightforward: make the package the hotel already built visible and usable to the guests it was designed for.
Frequently asked questions

We already announced the package to every department. Isn't that promotion? Internal announcement means the hotel knows. Promotion means the guest knows, understands the fit, and can use it. They're different jobs.

Our ad already lists all the benefits. Why isn't that enough? A benefit list tells guests what they get, but not whether it's for them. Without a clear segment and scenario, most readers don't feel addressed and move on.

If a guest booked the package, don't they obviously know what's included? Not always. Many guests book on price or a headline perk, then arrive unsure how to redeem the rest. The confirmation and pre-arrival messages have to carry the usage details.

Should staff push the package to every caller? No. The point is matching, not pushing. Staff should recognize which guest situations the package fits and offer it there, which is why the introduction card focuses on fit rather than a script.

How do we know if the fix worked? Track promotion in layers rather than by launch date: reach, page inquiries, staff recommendations, guest understanding, redemption, on-site fulfillment, and review feedback. The layer where numbers drop tells you where to work next.
Keywords: hotel package sales, hotel marketing, hotel staff training
